Standing Committee on Economics
18/09/2026
Review of the Reserve Bank of Australia Annual Report 2025

BULLOCK, Ms Michele, Governor, Reserve Bank of Australia

HAUSER, Mr Andrew, Deputy Governor, Reserve Bank of Australia

HUNTER, Dr Sarah, Assistant Governor, Economic, Reserve Bank of Australia

JONES, Dr Brad, Assistant Governor, Financial System, Reserve Bank of Australia

Committee met at 09:30

CHAIR ( Mr Husic ): Welcome. I declare open this hearing of the House of Representatives Standing Committee on Economics for the review of the Reserve Bank of Australia:annual report 2025. I want to begin by acknowledging the Ngunnawal and Ngambri peoples, who are the traditional custodians of the lands on which we meet today, and pay my respects to elders past and present, and I also extend that respect to any Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples joining us today.

The hearing comes at a consequential time for the Australian and world economies. Our economy has continued to grow in difficult global circumstances. The latest national accounts show that real GDP increased by 0.4 per cent in the June quarter and 2.1 per cent over the year, with growth increasingly supported by private demand.

Ms Bullock : Sure. I might start with the second part first because I think that's what's influencing a lot of what's going on overseas. When the conflict first started, there was, I think, if you like, a baseline assumption—certainly on our part and amongst many other countries—that it would be short-lived and that the rise in oil prices and associated fuel prices and other energy prices would be short-lived and they would ultimately come back down—maybe not to pre-conflict levels but that they would certainly come back.

CHAIR: Thanks so much, Governor. In my opening statement, I referenced the US Federal Reserve decision to raise interest rates by 25 basis points yesterday. It appears to be an important moment to obtain the observations of the RBA about what's happening in the global economy, particularly as it affects our trading partners. I wonder if you could reflect on any implications of that decision and, additionally, what the re-escalation of conflict in the Middle East has meant for global interest rates.

Ms Bullock : Yes. Certainly, over the past period since the conflict started, we have seen expectations for interest rates to rise in all countries. Initially at least in the US it was a bit different. They priced in falls and then they just priced in no falls, whereas other countries started to price in rises. With the prolonged Middle East conflict, what we're seeing now is that even in the United States there are predictions by markets for increases in interest rates. We're seeing the same thing in Australia.

Mr KENNEDY: You just enunciated, which was helpful, that public demand is driven by not only payments, public payments, but investments and all those things.

Mr Hauser : Could I add one thing, Chair, and you can tell me to shut up if you don't want me to, but—

Proceedings suspended from 10:54 to 11:05

Mr GREGG: With the distributional effects, we saw some spending data from NAB that indicated that there's very robust spending across age brackets but particularly in the under-25 and over-65 age demographics, which seem to be less sensitive to interest rate changes. Is the distributional effect of interest rate changes itself changing? And will that impact the effectiveness of these levers long term?

Ms Bullock : On the AI boom, there are certainly some issues around financial stability that some are concerned about. Globally, if you look at some of the things people are concerned about, they're concerned about the possibility that asset prices have run up quite quickly. We can talk about financial stability. I could call on Brad to talk about that a bit.

Committee adjourned at 12:30
